source.title: How does a Neural Network's Architecture Impact its Robustness to Noisy Labels?
source.authors: Jing-Ling Li; Mozhi Zhang; Keyulu Xu; John P. Dickerson; Jimmy Ba

record.tranche_reason: Tests how noisy-label training affects networks using standard training and representation-based measures; its architecture comparisons and robustness measure differ from the original studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on CIFAR-Easy with 100% uniform label noise. Its general statement that models were trained until close to 100% training accuracy supports interpreting these endpoint results as fitting noisy labels. Other results on learned representations do not directly measure the claim versions. The paper’s references to prior studies are not extracted as results.
record.test_reason: Standard SGD training and raw training/test accuracy across uniform-label-noise fractions directly test V4. The extracted 100% endpoints are instance-dependent noise, not completely random labels, so they do not establish V1.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that architecture alignment with target and noise functions affects the predictive power retained in representations, with theoretical support in a simplified setting and empirical support across graph and vision tasks.
record.recipe_differences: Uses standard SGD-based training on image datasets with synthetic label noise, including a 100% uniform-noise condition; evaluates test accuracy and predictive power in learned representations rather than focusing on the original studies’ random-label fitting claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that outcomes depend on architecture alignment, dataset, noise type, and noise ratio.

fits_no_version.finding: At 100% instance-dependent noise, vanilla MLP and CNN achieve 10.25% and 10.07% accuracy on CIFAR-Easy's pixel-location target.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fitting structured alternative labels can yield chance performance on the original target.

fits_no_version.finding: Predictive power measured using clean-label linear probes depends on architecture alignment with target and noise functions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architectural alignment affects how much target information remains linearly recoverable after noisy-label training.

record.problems: The 100% noise endpoint is reported for CIFAR-Easy; the paper does not establish the result across standard image datasets generally. Training accuracy is described as close to 100%, not given as a condition-specific number in Table 2. The broader noise-ratio trends appear in figures without extractable values here.
record.rows_left_out: Figure-only curves in Figures 7 and 8, including the CIFAR-Easy noise-ratio sweeps relevant to V4, were not extracted as condition-specific rows because the text gives no corresponding per-condition values. Other reported predictive-power measures do not directly test the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: No completely uniform-random-label endpoint is reported; the uniform-noise tables stop at 90%.
No comparison of convergence times or training trajectories across noise fractions.
No training on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
The 100% uniform-noise endpoint and condition-specific numerical training accuracies are unreported; near-perfect training fit is stated collectively.
No complete random-label fitting experiment or regularization-removal comparison. Weight decay and CNN dropout are present, but their necessity and sufficiency are not isolated.
No measurements of whether clean patterns are learned before noisy labels.

missing.what: Vanilla uniform-noise test-accuracy sweeps for all three architectures on CIFAR-10/100. Table 1 supplies numerical results through 90%; Tables 5 and 7 additionally provide clean-label ResNet18 baselines and uncertainties. These numerical results were not declared omitted by the figure-only exclusion.
CIFAR-Easy vanilla uniform-noise rows: MLP 100.00%, 99.88%, 97.57%, 86.29%; CNN 100.00%, 81.08%, 10.15%, 10.36%, at 0%, 50%, 80%, 90% noise respectively.

Training-fit evidence: Section 4 states that the vision models were trained to close to 100% training accuracy. Record this separately from test accuracy, retaining its collective rather than condition-specific precision.

record.verdict_notes: The decisive extraction error is Table 2 column attribution: its 100% column belongs to spurious noise. Uniform-noise columns end at 90%. Linear-probe and DivideMix improvements do not themselves establish the listed memorization claims.

versions.untested_parts: Tests a 100% uniform-noise endpoint on CIFAR-Easy, not completely random labels across standard image datasets or all architectures and hyperparameter settings.
Training time and how convergence changes with corrupted-label fraction are not reported.
Does not train on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

The study varies noise ratios and reports test accuracy in figures, but the figure-only curves do not provide extractable condition-specific values here. It does not report the full claimed combination of perfect training fit and steadily rising test error as text or table values.
Does not test whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation prevent fitting random labels, or whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
Does not measure the order in which real patterns and noisy labels are learned over training.

rows.subject: 4-layer FC (MLP)
rows.operation_detail: Vanilla training on CIFAR-Easy with uniform label noise at 100% noise ratio.
rows.note: The paper says models in this section were trained until they could fit noisy labels, achieving close to 100% training accuracy. The 10.25% test accuracy is near the 10-class chance level implied by the paper’s CIFAR-Easy setup.
rows.check: 10.25% is the vanilla MLP result at 100% spurious/instance-dependent noise in Table 2. Labels are original CIFAR-10 image classes replacing pixel-location labels, not uniform random labels. Chance performance on the pixel-location task therefore does not establish V1.

rows.subject: 9-layer CNN
rows.operation_detail: Vanilla training on CIFAR-Easy with uniform label noise at 100% noise ratio.
rows.note: The paper says models in this section were trained until they could fit noisy labels, achieving close to 100% training accuracy. The 10.07% test accuracy is near the 10-class chance level implied by the paper’s CIFAR-Easy setup.
rows.check: 10.07% is the vanilla CNN result at 100% spurious/instance-dependent noise in Table 2, not 100% uniform noise. These structured image-class labels do not test fitting completely random labels.

relationships.condition: Vanilla MLP, CNN, and PreAct ResNet18 on CIFAR-10/100 with increasing uniform noise through 90%
relationships.reason: From text and missing table rows: models reportedly reach near-perfect training accuracy while test accuracy decreases at each reported noise fraction; ResNet18 falls from 95.0% to 17.2% on CIFAR-10 and 77.1% to 3.9% on CIFAR-100.
relationships.display_finding: Training accuracy was nearly perfect while test accuracy declined at every reported noise level, with ResNet18 falling from 95.0% to 17.2% on CIFAR-10 and from 77.1% to 3.9% on CIFAR-100.

relationships.display_finding: Nearly perfect training fit accompanied test accuracies of 100.00%, 99.88%, 97.57%, and 86.29%, preserving substantial predictive signal.

relationships.condition: Vanilla CNN on CIFAR-Easy with uniform noise
relationships.reason: From missing Table 2 rows: despite reportedly near-perfect training fit, test accuracy drops from 81.08% at 50% noise to chance at 80% (10.15%) and remains there at 90% (10.36%); degradation includes an early collapse rather than sustained recovery of remaining signal.
relationships.display_finding: Despite near-perfect training fit, test accuracy fell from 81.08% at 50% noise to 10.15% at 80% and 10.36% at 90%.

source_check.reason: Table 2 shows 81.08% accuracy at 50% noise, 10.15% at 80%, and 10.36% at 90%, despite the reported near-perfect training fit. This qualifies the claimed steady degradation and retention of remaining signal.
